title: Microbatch pipeline aperture sampling study
summary: Working notes for an experiment exploring how microbatch start-phase ("aperture") alignment impacts GPU occupancy, kernel handoff jitter, and tail latency. Uses phase-shifted Nsight Systems traces and repeated captures with and without CUDA graph capture to isolate scheduling-related variability.
background_and_motivation: We've observed intermittent 99th percentile tail latency spikes on multi-request workloads that otherwise have good median latency. Previous Nsight runs focused on kernel-level stalls and SM occupancy, but several traces hinted at a temporal alignment effect: when multiple microbatches start at similar scheduler epochs, we see short-lived contention and transient occupancy degradation. This doc captures a structured experiment to quantify that 'aperture' effect and propose mitigations.
hypothesis: If microbatch starts are tightly phase-aligned (small aperture), kernel launch storms create transient L2/cache pressure and streaming multiprocessor contention that reduces achieved occupancy for a short window, increasing tail latency. Staggering microbatch starts (increasing aperture) should smooth demand and reduce peak contention, at the cost of slightly higher median latency if serialization increases.
experiment_setup: Hardware: 2x NVIDIA A100-SXM (80GB) on a 4-socket machine. CUDA 12.1, driver 535.xx. Nsight Systems 2028.6 for timeline traces, Nsight Compute 2028.6 for kernel counters. Model: open-architecture 7B autoregressive model (decoder-only) with kv-cache enabled. Workload: 120 concurrent client threads issuing single-turn generation requests; seq_in=64, seq_out=128; model batcher microbatch sizes varied: [1, 2, 4]. Batcher window: 6ms target horizon. Test variants: (A) phase-aligned: force batcher to flush microbatches at the boundary (tight aperture ~0–1ms), (B) staggered: insert randomized jitter up to 8ms per microbatch start (aperture ~0–8ms), (C) cuda-graph-capture: same as (A) but with CUDA graph capture enabled for persistent execution path. Each variant repeated 10 times to capture variance. Tracing: NVTX around batcher handoff, mark microbatch id and phase offset. Collected per-run: Nsight Systems timeline, Nsight Compute aggregated counters for attn_fwd_k and ff_fwd_k kernels, system metrics (SM utilization, L2 bw, dram bw).
measurements_and_metrics: Primary metrics: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (tokens/s), achieved_occupancy (per-kernel from Nsight Compute), warp_efficiency, L2 cache util, nsight timeline handoff jitter (ms). Secondary: number of persistent kernel context-switches, kernel queue length at launch, CUDA-graph replay variance. We log per-microbatch delta between scheduled start and actual kernel-first-launch.
results_summary:
Key observations across runs:

- Phase-aligned (A): reproducible short pulses of reduced achieved_occupancy for attn_fwd_k and ff_fwd_k lasting ~3–7ms at ~200–400ms intervals (depends on batcher behavior). p99 increased by ~18% vs median and we observed 3–6% throughput drop compared to staggered.
- Staggered (B): occupancy curves flatten; achieved_occupancy per kernel rises by ~6–12 percentage points during previously-observed pulses. p99 latency improved by ~12% relative to (A). Overall tokens/s improved by ~2–4%.
- CUDA-graph-capture (C): median latency improved (fewer kernel launch overheads) but the short occupancy pulses in (A) persisted, though with smaller amplitude. p99 remained higher than (B) in 7/10 runs. CUDA graphs reduce launch overhead variance but do not eliminate contention caused by simultaneous memory traffic bursts.

Numeric excerpt (representative run):
- Variant A (aligned): median latency 38.2ms, p95 62.1ms, p99 110.5ms, tokens/s 24.1k
- Variant B (staggered): median latency 39.7ms, p95 59.0ms, p99 97.0ms, tokens/s 25.0k
- Variant C (cuda-graph): median 34.9ms, p95 61.0ms, p99 103.2ms, tokens/s 24.6k

Counters (attn_fwd_k): achieved_occupancy drop from 76% -> 59% in aligned pulses; warp_efficiency drop from 92% -> 80%. L2 read BW spikes correlate with pulse windows (up to +40% over baseline).
trace_notes_and_artifacts:
Representative Nsight Systems timeline shows microbatch handoff NVTX events coalescing at t=~0.8s producing a 4ms window where multiple kernels queue up and memory copy streams (async copies) compete with compute due to similar priority. We observed the following patterns in multiple traces:

- Kernel launch storm: 10–12 kernel launches within a 2ms window.
- Async copy completion bursts that coincide with kernel queue bursts.
- Persistent kernels (when enabled) reduced kernel-launch-throttling but still suffered from L2 thrash when many microbatches fetch kv-slices concurrently.

Attached artifacts: links above; Nsight zip snapshots stored in PR #3124 artifacts (see link).
interpretation: The aperture effect looks real: when microbatch starts align, the instantaneous demand on on-chip resources (L2, SM registers allocation peaks, and DRAM requests) creates short intervals of reduced execution efficiency for the most critical kernels. CUDA graph capture reduces CPU-side overhead but does not avoid on-device contention originating from simultaneous microbatch memory access patterns.
short_term_mitigations: 1) Add configurable 'aperture jitter' in the batcher to spread microbatch start times by up to N ms (default 4ms). 2) Introduce a probabilistic staggering policy: if N concurrent microbatches > threshold, apply jitter. 3) Lower priority of background async copy streams that are not latency-critical during high-concurrency windows. 4) For dedicated instances, enable prewarm persistent-kernel mode to reduce kernel rebound effects.
longer_term_recommendations: 1) Rework KV prefetch to allow cooperative prefetch windows: decouple kv-slices fetch from immediate kernel launch where possible. 2) Investigate microbatch-aware memory scheduling on the runtime (track in INF-1310). 3) Explore adaptive aperture control based on telemetry: detect onset of kernel-launch storms via short-time-window counters and inject staggering automatically. 4) Add a small experiment to test interleaving microbatch KV ranges to reduce simultaneous hotset reads.
unresolved_questions_and_next_steps:
- How does aperture interact with multi-model serving on the same GPU? (likely exacerbates L2 thrash)
- What is the optimum default jitter window for different model sizes and sequence lengths? Need a grid sweep.
- Can hardware-level QoS (stream priorities + preemptible compute streams) be tuned to mitigate the pulses without degrading throughput?

Next steps: implement an internal flag in batcher to enable stochastic aperture jitter (PR linked), run extended soak tests for 24h with jitter enabled, and measure p99 stability. Also schedule a follow-up Nsight sweep focusing on L2 bank conflict counters and DRAM request concurrency (Ms TO-DO).
notes_to_self: Capture a second set of traces with NVTX marking both kv-prefetch and the copy-complete callbacks to pin down exact ordering differences. Ask SRE to reserve a non-shared GPU node for a long-run test (no noisy neighbors). Compare results versus a smaller model (3B) to see scaling behavior.
